title: PostgreSQL DBA Part 26: Reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
description: Learn to read PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE with BUFFERS: cost vs actual rows, loops, shared hit and read, temp files and heap fetches, with real plans.

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: Index-Only Scans and Covering Indexes

reviewNotes: Series part 26. Publish Part 25 first (Part 25 and Parts 19-24 are not live yet; Part 25 is named without a link and is not in related). TEST ENVIRONMENT: PostgreSQL 18 could NOT be installed in this sandbox. postgresql-18 is available from PGDG but depends on liburing2 from the Ubuntu archive, which the sandbox network blocks (apt: 'postgresql-18 : Depends: liburing2 (>= 2.5) but it is not installable'). Following the task instructions, every SQL statement was run exactly as written on the distribution PostgreSQL 16.15 (Ubuntu 16.15-0ubuntu0.24.04.1) on Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, cluster 16 main; all plan outputs are real output from that server, captioned '(expected output)'. Documentation followed: PostgreSQL 18 pages (/docs/18/). Note that postgresql.org/docs/current/ now serves PostgreSQL 19 documentation (it lists an EXPLAIN IO option that does not exist in 18), so I used the /docs/18/ URLs in sources. KNOWN PG 18 DIFFERENCES the editor should check by re-running on 18 and replacing the plan outputs: (1) actual rows print with two decimals (rows=33.33 loops=3); (2) Index Scan/Bitmap Index Scan/Index Only Scan nodes add an 'Index Searches: N' line; (3) BUFFERS is automatic with ANALYZE (the article writes BUFFERS explicitly, which is valid on 18); (4) PostgreSQL 18 uses asynchronous I/O (io_method), so cold-cache 'shared read' timings in Steps 3-4 may look different. Costs, estimated rows and buffer counts should match for the same data. Also check: the three error messages in Common mistakes were captured on 16 (texts match the 18 source to my knowledge but were not run on 18); the systemd unit postgresql@18-main and the path /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_test_timing are written for 18 per the series platform. The work_mem example honestly shows the in-memory sort was slightly slower on the test machine (temp files stayed in OS cache); the text explains this rather than claiming a speed-up.

data.text: This is Part 26 of the PostgreSQL DBA series. In Part 25 we used pg_stat_statements to find the statements that cost the server the most time. Now you need to know why they are slow, and that is what EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) tells you. By the end of this part you will be able to run it safely, read every important line of the output, and turn what you see into a fix: an index, fresh statistics, more work_mem or a VACUUM.

The short answer: EXPLAIN shows the plan PostgreSQL intends to use, with estimated costs and row counts. Adding ANALYZE really runs the query and adds the actual time, rows and loops for every step. BUFFERS adds how many 8 kB pages each step found in memory (hit) or had to read from the operating system (read). On PostgreSQL 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes the buffer numbers automatically.
What you will learn

items.content: How a query plan is built as a tree of nodes, and which order to read it in.
The difference between estimated cost and rows and the actual time, rows and loops.
What shared hit, shared read, temp read/written and I/O Timings tell a DBA.
How to spot the classic problems: missing index, stale statistics, sorts spilling to disk, too many heap fetches and loop multiplication.
How to run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on UPDATE and DELETE without changing data, and how to explain queries copied from pg_stat_statements that contain $1.

data.text: Prerequisites

items.content: Parts 1 to 25 of this series. You will use ideas from Part 11 (MVCC), Part 12 (VACUUM and the visibility map) and Part 25 (pg_stat_statements).
One Ubuntu server, called db1 in this part, with PostgreSQL 18 from the PGDG repository and the default cluster 18 main on port 5432, installed as in Part 2.
A user with sudo rights. Every SQL step runs in psql as the postgres superuser, which connects through peer authentication.
About 100 MB of free disk space for the practice database. Use a test server, not production, because some steps restart PostgreSQL.

data.text: How it works

When you send a query, the planner (the part of PostgreSQL that decides how to run a query) considers several ways to get the answer and picks the one it thinks is cheapest. The result is a plan: a tree of steps called nodes. Each node does one job, such as reading a table (Seq Scan), using an index (Index Scan), joining two inputs (Nested Loop, Hash Join) or sorting (Sort).

Think of it like a navigation app. Before you leave, it shows a route and an estimated travel time. That is plain EXPLAIN. If you actually drive the route and write down how long each stretch took, that is EXPLAIN ANALYZE. A big gap between the estimate and the real trip tells you where the app's map (the table statistics) is wrong.
Read a plan from the inside out. The most indented nodes run first and pass rows up to their parent, marked with ->. The top line is the last step and its numbers include everything below it.
Every node line has the same parts:

content: Estimated startup cost (work before the first row comes out) and total cost (work to return all rows). The unit is arbitrary, based on settings such as seq_page_cost, not milliseconds.
Estimated number of rows this node returns (not how many it reads).
Estimated average size of one output row, in bytes.
Real milliseconds to the first row and to the last row, per loop. Only with ANALYZE.
Real rows returned, averaged per loop. Only with ANALYZE.
How many times the node ran. Multiply actual time and rows by loops to get the totals.
8 kB pages found in PostgreSQL's shared buffer cache (hit) or read from the operating system (read), for this node and all its children.

data.text: Under the node line you see detail lines, for example Filter and Rows Removed by Filter (rows that were read and then thrown away), Sort Method (in memory or on disk), Heap Fetches (table visits during an index-only scan) and, at the bottom, Planning Time and Execution Time.
What changed in PostgreSQL 18

items.content: BUFFERS is automatic with ANALYZE. EXPLAIN ANALYZE now prints the Buffers lines without asking. Before PostgreSQL 18 you had to write EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). This part writes BUFFERS explicitly so the commands work the same on older versions.
Fractional row counts. Actual rows are shown with two decimals, for example rows=33.33 loops=3. Older versions round this to rows=33, which hides small per-loop numbers.
Index Searches. Index Scan, Bitmap Index Scan and Index Only Scan nodes print an Index Searches: N line with the total number of index lookups across all loops.

More detail elsewhere: the WAL option also reports how often WAL buffers became full, Material, Window Aggregate and CTE nodes report memory and disk use, and disabled nodes are marked Disabled: true.

data.title: About the outputs in this part
data.text: The commands below are written for PostgreSQL 18. The plan outputs were captured on a test machine and are marked as expected output: on PostgreSQL 18 your actual rows will show two decimals (rows=100.00) and index scan nodes will have an extra Index Searches line. Timings will differ on every machine, but costs, row counts and buffer counts should be the same or very close if you load the same data.
Set up a practice database
Step 1: Create the shop database and sample tables
On db1, as your sudo user. The commands switch to the postgres operating system user: first create the database from the shell, then connect to it with psql.

data.code:
sudo -u postgres createdb shop
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop
data.caption: Create and connect to the practice database

data.text: Now create two tables. The data is generated with simple arithmetic instead of random numbers, so you get exactly the same rows and the same plans as shown here. Customer 42 has 100 orders; one order in every hundred is pending.

data.caption: Sample tables: 5,000 customers and 500,000 orders

data.code:
CREATE TABLE
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 5000
INSERT 0 500000
VACUUM
data.caption: Output

data.text: VACUUM ANALYZE at the end collects fresh statistics, so the planner starts with an accurate picture of the tables. To verify, check the page and row counts the planner will use:

data.code: SELECT relpages, reltuples FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders';
data.caption: Verify: planner statistics for orders
Output

data.text: The orders table fills 3,677 pages of 8 kB and holds 500,000 rows. Keep these two numbers in mind for the next step.
Read a plan without running the query
Step 2: Run plain EXPLAIN

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. Plain EXPLAIN only plans the query. It does not run it, so it is safe on any statement, even on a busy production server.

data.code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
data.caption: Show the estimated plan

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..7291.17 rows=100 width=30)
   Workers Planned: 2
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6281.17 rows=42 width=30)
         Filter: (customer_id = 42)
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: Read it from the inside out. The bottom node is a Parallel Seq Scan: each process reads part of the table and keeps rows where customer_id = 42. Workers Planned: 2 means two background worker processes help the main process (the leader). The Gather node on top collects their rows. The planner expects 100 rows in total, about 42 per process.

Where does the cost come from? For a plain sequential scan the documentation's formula is: pages × seq_page_cost (default 1.0) + rows × cpu_tuple_cost (default 0.01) + rows × cpu_operator_cost (default 0.0025) for the filter. You can check it by turning parallel query off for your session only:

data.caption: Verify: the non-parallel cost

data.code:
SET
                         QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------
 Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..9927.00 rows=100 width=30)
   Filter: (customer_id = 42)
(2 rows)

RESET
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: 3,677 × 1.0 + 500,000 × 0.01 + 500,000 × 0.0025 = 3,677 + 5,000 + 1,250 = 9,927, exactly the total cost shown. The parallel plan was estimated at 7,291, so the planner chose it. This is the whole idea of the planner: it compares estimated costs and picks the lowest.
Run the query with ANALYZE and BUFFERS

data.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement
data.text: With ANALYZE the statement is executed. For a SELECT that means the full work and load on the server, only the result rows are thrown away. For INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE and CREATE TABLE AS the data really changes. Step 10 shows the safe way. On production, never run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a query that already takes minutes without thinking about the extra load.
Step 3: Compare a cold run and a warm run
On db1, as your sudo user, restart the cluster so PostgreSQL's cache (shared buffers) is empty. Do this on a test server only.

data.code:
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop
data.caption: Restart the cluster (test server only) and reconnect

data.text: Then, in psql as postgres, run the same query twice with ANALYZE and BUFFERS:

data.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
data.caption: Run the query twice

content: Carries out the command and shows actual run times and other statistics.
Shows shared, local and temp blocks hit, read, dirtied and written. Automatic with ANALYZE on PostgreSQL 18.

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..7291.17 rows=100 width=30) (actual time=0.850..44.557 rows=100 loops=1)
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   Buffers: shared read=3677
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6281.17 rows=42 width=30) (actual time=1.271..37.439 rows=33 loops=3)
         Filter: (customer_id = 42)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 166633
         Buffers: shared read=3677
 Planning Time: 0.040 ms
 Execution Time: 44.590 ms
(10 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line), first run

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..7291.17 rows=100 width=30) (actual time=0.141..14.726 rows=100 loops=1)
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   Buffers: shared hit=3677
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6281.17 rows=42 width=30) (actual time=0.018..10.150 rows=33 loops=3)
         Filter: (customer_id = 42)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 166633
         Buffers: shared hit=3677
 Planning Time: 0.051 ms
 Execution Time: 14.746 ms
(10 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line), second run

data.text: Look at three things. First, Buffers: shared read=3677 in the first run and shared hit=3677 in the second: the same 3,677 pages, first read from the operating system, then found in PostgreSQL's cache. The execution time dropped from about 45 ms to about 15 ms only because of that.

Second, rows=33 loops=3 on the Parallel Seq Scan. The node ran three times (the leader plus two workers) and returned about 33 rows each time: 33 × 3 ≈ 100, which matches the Gather node. On PostgreSQL 18 this line reads rows=33.33 loops=3. Rows Removed by Filter: 166633 is also a per-process average: almost 500,000 rows were read and thrown away to find 100.
Third, the estimate (rows=100) and the actual result (100 rows) agree, so the statistics are good. The plan is slow because it reads the whole table, not because the planner was misled.

data.title: Always run a query twice when you measure
data.text: The first run after a restart, or for data nobody touched for a while, pays for reading pages from disk. Look at the shared read count, not just the time. If a production query is slow and shows a high read count, the data is not in memory; if it shows a high hit count, the query simply touches too many pages.
Step 4: Measure time spent on I/O with track_io_timing

The read count tells you how many pages came from outside PostgreSQL, not how long they took. The setting track_io_timing adds that. Its default is off, because it asks the operating system for the current time repeatedly, which can add noticeable overhead on some platforms. Only superusers and roles with the SET privilege on it can change it, so here you turn it on for your own session only. Restart the cluster again first (test server only) so the cache is cold:

data.code:
sudo systemctl restart postgresql@18-main
sudo -u postgres psql -d shop
data.caption: Restart and reconnect (test server only)

data.code:
SET track_io_timing = on;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
data.caption: Turn on I/O timing for this session

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Gather  (cost=1000.00..7291.17 rows=100 width=30) (actual time=0.666..43.868 rows=100 loops=1)
   Workers Planned: 2
   Workers Launched: 2
   Buffers: shared read=3677
   I/O Timings: shared read=78.441
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6281.17 rows=42 width=30) (actual time=0.233..35.621 rows=33 loops=3)
         Filter: (customer_id = 42)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 166633
         Buffers: shared read=3677
         I/O Timings: shared read=78.441
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=55 read=17
   I/O Timings: shared read=0.852
 Planning Time: 1.927 ms
 Execution Time: 44.236 ms
(15 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: I/O Timings: shared read=78.441 is the time in milliseconds spent waiting for those 3,677 reads. It is larger than the 44 ms execution time because it adds up the waits of all three processes, which ran at the same time. The Planning: section shows that even planning needed to read 17 pages of system catalog data after the restart.
To check how expensive timing is on your hardware before you enable it for the whole server, run /usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin/pg_test_timing. If the overhead is low, many DBAs enable it permanently:

data.caption: Optional: enable for the whole cluster (reload, no restart)

data.text: A reload is enough for this parameter. To undo it, run ALTER SYSTEM RESET track_io_timing; and SELECT pg_reload_conf();. With it on, pg_stat_statements (Part 25) and pg_stat_database (Part 24) also fill their I/O time columns.
Use the plan to fix a query
Step 5: Add an index and compare the plans

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. The plan in Step 3 read 3,677 pages and threw away almost 500,000 rows to return 100. That pattern (a big Rows Removed by Filter on a Seq Scan for a selective condition) is the classic sign of a missing index.

data.code:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
data.caption: Create the index and explain again

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=5.20..353.71 rows=100 width=30) (actual time=0.019..0.068 rows=100 loops=1)
   Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 42)
   Heap Blocks: exact=100
   Buffers: shared hit=103
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx  (cost=0.00..5.17 rows=100 width=0) (actual time=0.008..0.008 rows=100 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
         Buffers: shared hit=3
 Planning Time: 0.036 ms
 Execution Time: 0.079 ms
(9 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line), second run after the index

data.text: Now the plan has two nodes. The Bitmap Index Scan reads the index (3 pages) and builds a list of table pages that contain matching rows. The Bitmap Heap Scan then visits those pages. Heap Blocks: exact=100 says the 100 rows sit on 100 different pages, which is true for this data: orders for one customer are spread across the table. On PostgreSQL 18 the Bitmap Index Scan also shows Index Searches: 1.

Verify the fix with the numbers: 103 buffers instead of 3,677, and an execution time of 0.079 ms instead of about 15 ms. Buffers are the more reliable comparison, because they do not change with machine speed or cache state.
Step 6: Catch a bad row estimate caused by stale statistics

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. The planner trusts the statistics that ANALYZE (or autovacuum) collects. If a table changes a lot and the statistics are not refreshed yet, the estimates are wrong, and wrong estimates lead to wrong plans. To show this, switch autovacuum off for this table only and load 50,000 cancelled orders, a status the statistics have never seen:

data.caption: Load new data without refreshing statistics

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate  (cost=7993.60..7993.61 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=17.367..20.100 rows=1 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=4094
   ->  Gather  (cost=1000.00..7993.60 rows=1 width=0) (actual time=11.152..17.546 rows=50000 loops=1)
         Workers Planned: 2
         Workers Launched: 2
         Buffers: shared hit=4094
         ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6993.50 rows=1 width=0) (actual time=9.018..11.442 rows=16667 loops=3)
               Filter: (status = 'cancelled'::text)
               Rows Removed by Filter: 166667
               Buffers: shared hit=4094
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=12 read=4
 Planning Time: 0.276 ms
 Execution Time: 20.119 ms
(14 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: Compare estimate and actual on the Parallel Seq Scan: the planner expected rows=1 but each process returned 16,667 rows, 50,000 in total. An error of this size is the most important thing to look for in any plan. Here it does no harm, because a full scan is the right plan anyway, but in a join the same mistake can make the planner choose a nested loop that runs 50,000 times instead of once.

data.caption: Refresh statistics and check again

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate  (cost=8010.76..8010.77 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=13.768..16.645 rows=1 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=4094
   ->  Gather  (cost=8010.55..8010.76 rows=2 width=8) (actual time=13.677..16.639 rows=3 loops=1)
         Workers Planned: 2
         Workers Launched: 2
         Buffers: shared hit=4094
         ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=7010.55..7010.56 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=11.725..11.725 rows=1 loops=3)
               Buffers: shared hit=4094
               ->  Parallel Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..6958.58 rows=20785 width=0) (actual time=8.880..10.796 rows=16667 loops=3)
                     Filter: (status = 'cancelled'::text)
                     Rows Removed by Filter: 166667
                     Buffers: shared hit=4094
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=22
 Planning Time: 0.123 ms
 Execution Time: 16.670 ms
(16 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: After ANALYZE the per-process estimate is 20,785, now the right size, and the planner changes the plan shape: each worker counts its own rows (Partial Aggregate) and the leader adds the three results (Finalize Aggregate). Keep autovacuum off for now, Step 9 needs it; you switch it back on there.
Spot the classic problems
Step 7: Multiply by loops in a nested loop join

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. In a Nested Loop join, the inner node (the second child) runs once for every row from the outer node. Its numbers are per loop, and forgetting to multiply them is the most common reading mistake.

data.code:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT c.full_name, o.order_id, o.amount
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 WHERE c.customer_id BETWEEN 100 AND 109
   AND o.status = 'pending';
data.caption: Pending orders for ten customers

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Nested Loop  (cost=5.53..3509.66 rows=11 width=27) (actual time=0.129..0.690 rows=100 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=1133
   ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c  (cost=0.28..8.48 rows=10 width=17) (actual time=0.004..0.007 rows=10 loops=1)
         Index Cond: ((customer_id >= 100) AND (customer_id <= 109))
         Buffers: shared hit=3
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders o  (cost=5.25..350.11 rows=1 width=18) (actual time=0.061..0.066 rows=10 loops=10)
         Recheck Cond: (c.customer_id = customer_id)
         Filter: (status = 'pending'::text)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 100
         Heap Blocks: exact=1100
         Buffers: shared hit=1130
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx  (cost=0.00..5.25 rows=110 width=0) (actual time=0.004..0.004 rows=110 loops=10)
               Index Cond: (customer_id = c.customer_id)
               Buffers: shared hit=30
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=103 read=2 dirtied=1
 Planning Time: 0.589 ms
 Execution Time: 0.812 ms
(18 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: The outer Index Scan on customers returns 10 rows, so the inner Bitmap Heap Scan on orders runs loops=10. Its rows=10 is an average: 10 × 10 = 100 rows in total, which matches the top node. Rows Removed by Filter: 100 is also per loop, so 1,000 orders were read and discarded. Heap Blocks: exact=1100 and the Buffers line are already totals for all loops.

Now look at the estimate: rows=1 per loop against 10 actual. The planner treats customer and status as independent, but in this data all 100 pending orders belong to one customer (101). An average of 10 hides that fact: one loop returned 100 rows and nine returned none. When numbers like this matter, extended statistics (Part 32) can teach the planner about related columns.
Step 8: See a sort spill to disk and fix it with work_mem

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. Sorts and hash tables may use up to work_mem of memory each (default 4MB; hash operations can use hash_mem_multiplier times that, default 2.0). If the data does not fit, PostgreSQL writes it to temporary files. EXPLAIN shows this in two places.

data.caption: Sort all 550,000 orders with the default work_mem

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Sort  (cost=75193.95..76568.95 rows=550000 width=30) (actual time=462.127..614.122 rows=550000 loops=1)
   Sort Key: amount DESC, order_id
   Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 22184kB
   Buffers: shared hit=4094, temp read=2773 written=2784
   ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..9594.00 rows=550000 width=30) (actual time=0.002..37.466 rows=550000 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared hit=4094
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=15
 Planning Time: 0.052 ms
 Execution Time: 648.005 ms
(10 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: Sort Method: external merge Disk: 22184kB means the sort did not fit in 4 MB and used about 22 MB of temporary files. The Buffers line confirms it with temp read=2773 written=2784: temporary blocks written and read back. Now give this session more memory and run it again:

data.caption: Same sort with 64MB of work_mem

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Sort  (cost=62033.95..63408.95 rows=550000 width=30) (actual time=656.370..728.560 rows=550000 loops=1)
   Sort Key: amount DESC, order_id
   Sort Method: quicksort  Memory: 50039kB
   Buffers: shared hit=4094
   ->  Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..9594.00 rows=550000 width=30) (actual time=0.008..38.421 rows=550000 loops=1)
         Buffers: shared hit=4094
 Planning Time: 0.125 ms
 Execution Time: 753.313 ms
(8 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: Verify: the sort now runs in memory (quicksort Memory: 50039kB) and the temp numbers are gone. Notice that the execution time did not improve on this test machine; it was a little slower. The temporary files were small and stayed in the operating system's file cache, so the disk sort was cheap. On a busy server with real disk I/O the in-memory sort usually wins, but this is exactly why you measure instead of assuming.

data.title: Do not raise work_mem for everyone at once
data.text: work_mem applies to each sort or hash operation, and one query can run several at the same time, in many sessions. Setting it to 64MB in postgresql.conf could use many times that amount of RAM under load. Raise it per session (SET work_mem) or per role (ALTER ROLE ... SET work_mem) for the reports that need it. Part 28 covers memory tuning in detail.
Step 9: Read Heap Fetches on an index-only scan

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. An Index Only Scan answers the query from the index alone, but only for table pages marked all-visible in the visibility map (a small file per table that VACUUM maintains, see Part 12). For other pages it must visit the table to check whether each row is visible to your transaction. Heap Fetches counts those table visits. Update some rows first, with autovacuum still off:

data.caption: Count rows right after an UPDATE

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate  (cost=4845.64..4845.65 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=31.461..31.462 rows=1 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=110087
   ->  Index Only Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders  (cost=0.42..4695.47 rows=60067 width=0) (actual time=0.466..28.200 rows=55000 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (customer_id <= 500)
         Heap Fetches: 110000
         Buffers: shared hit=110087
 Planning Time: 0.078 ms
 Execution Time: 31.486 ms
(8 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: The index-only scan returned 55,000 rows but made 110,000 heap fetches and touched 110,087 buffers. The UPDATE created new row versions and new index entries, while the old ones are still there (MVCC, Part 11), so PostgreSQL checked both. The buffer count is larger than the whole table because Buffers counts every access, not distinct pages.

data.caption: VACUUM, check again, and switch autovacuum back on

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Aggregate  (cost=1418.11..1418.12 rows=1 width=8) (actual time=6.965..6.965 rows=1 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=87
   ->  Index Only Scan using orders_customer_id_idx on orders  (cost=0.42..1282.89 rows=54084 width=0) (actual time=0.011..3.943 rows=55000 loops=1)
         Index Cond: (customer_id <= 500)
         Heap Fetches: 0
         Buffers: shared hit=87
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=12
 Planning Time: 0.103 ms
 Execution Time: 6.986 ms
(10 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: Verify: Heap Fetches: 0, 87 buffers instead of 110,087, and about 7 ms instead of 31 ms. When you see high Heap Fetches on a production table, check its vacuum history in pg_stat_user_tables before you touch the query. The last statement undoes the change from Step 6.
Explain writes and parameterised queries safely
Step 10: EXPLAIN ANALYZE an UPDATE inside a transaction

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. The documentation's advice for data-changing statements is to wrap them in a transaction and roll it back. The WAL option adds how much write-ahead log the statement produced, which matters for replication and backups (Parts 15 and 19).

data.caption: Measure an UPDATE without keeping its changes

content: Runs the UPDATE for real, so the measured numbers are real.
Shows pages hit, read, dirtied and written, including the pages the update changes.
Shows WAL records, full page images (fpi), bytes and, on PostgreSQL 18, how often WAL buffers were full. Only non-zero values are printed. Requires ANALYZE.

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Update on orders  (cost=5.24..388.70 rows=0 width=0) (actual time=1.121..1.121 rows=0 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=1309
   WAL: records=397 bytes=28490
   ->  Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=5.24..388.70 rows=1 width=38) (actual time=0.036..0.186 rows=100 loops=1)
         Recheck Cond: (customer_id = 101)
         Filter: (status = 'pending'::text)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 10
         Heap Blocks: exact=110
         Buffers: shared hit=113
         ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx  (cost=0.00..5.24 rows=109 width=0) (actual time=0.014..0.014 rows=110 loops=1)
               Index Cond: (customer_id = 101)
               Buffers: shared hit=3
 Planning:
   Buffers: shared hit=5
 Planning Time: 0.098 ms
 Execution Time: 1.148 ms
(16 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output: captured on PostgreSQL 16; on PostgreSQL 18 row counts show two decimals and index scans add an Index Searches line)

data.text: The Update node shows rows=0 because an UPDATE without RETURNING sends no rows back; the Bitmap Heap Scan below it found the 100 rows that were changed. WAL: records=397 bytes=28490 is the log volume for changing 100 rows and their index entries. No fpi value appears, which means no full page images were needed in this run.
Verify that nothing changed after the ROLLBACK:

data.code: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 101 AND status = 'pending';
data.caption: Verify the rows are still pending
Output

data.title: Statements that ROLLBACK cannot undo
data.text: BEGIN and ROLLBACK protect table data, but not everything. A sequence used by an INSERT stays advanced, and a statement that calls a function with outside effects (for example sending data with dblink) cannot be rolled back. Never run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a DELETE or UPDATE on production outside a transaction.
Step 11: Explain a query that contains $1 with GENERIC_PLAN

On db1, as the postgres operating system user, connected to the shop database with sudo -u postgres psql -d shop. Queries you copy from pg_stat_statements have their constants replaced by $1, $2 and so on. EXPLAIN cannot run them as they are, but the GENERIC_PLAN option (PostgreSQL 16 and later) plans them without values.

data.code: EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;
data.caption: Plan a parameterised query

data.code:
QUERY PLAN
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Bitmap Heap Scan on orders  (cost=5.27..388.46 rows=109 width=30)
   Recheck Cond: (customer_id = $1)
   ->  Bitmap Index Scan on orders_customer_id_idx  (cost=0.00..5.24 rows=109 width=0)
         Index Cond: (customer_id = $1)
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output (expected output)

data.text: This is the generic plan: the one PostgreSQL would use for a prepared statement without knowing the value. It cannot be combined with ANALYZE, because there is nothing to run. To measure real times, replace $1 with a typical value, ideally one taken from your application logs, and use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) as before.
A DBA's order for reading any plan
Plans for real queries can be a hundred lines long. Go through them in this order:

items.content: Execution Time at the bottom: is it really slow, and is Planning Time a surprise?
Estimated rows versus actual rows × loops on each node. Find the lowest node where they differ by ten times or more; that is usually the root cause.
Buffers: which node has the biggest jump in shared hit + read compared with its children? That node does the work.
Rows Removed by Filter much larger than the rows returned: a missing or unusable index.
temp read/written, Sort Method: external merge or Batches greater than 1 on a Hash node: work_mem is too small for this operation.
Heap Fetches close to the rows returned on an Index Only Scan: the table needs VACUUM.

data.text: For a plan you want to keep or compare later, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT JSON) gives the same information in a form that tools and scripts can read. EXPLAIN (SETTINGS) adds any planner-related setting that differs from its default, for example Settings: work_mem = '64MB', which is useful when you send a plan to a colleague.
Common mistakes and how to fix them
ERROR: EXPLAIN option WAL requires ANALYZE

data.code: EXPLAIN (WAL) DELETE FROM orders WHERE order_id = 1;
ERROR:  EXPLAIN option WAL requires ANALYZE
data.caption: Output

data.text: WAL, TIMING and SERIALIZE only make sense when the statement runs. Add ANALYZE, and for a DELETE like this one put it inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as in Step 10.
ERROR: there is no parameter $1

data.code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1;

data.caption: Output

data.text: The query came from pg_stat_statements or a log. Use EXPLAIN (GENERIC_PLAN) to see the plan, or replace the placeholders with real values to run it. Trying both at once gives ERROR: EXPLAIN options ANALYZE and GENERIC_PLAN cannot be used together.
Comparing cost with milliseconds
Cost is in planner units, actual time is in milliseconds, and they are not expected to match. Compare estimated rows with actual rows instead, and compare costs only between plans for the same query.
Forgetting to multiply by loops

A node with actual time=0.061..0.066 rows=10 loops=10 spent about 0.66 ms and returned 100 rows in total, not 0.066 ms and 10 rows. On the inner side of nested loops and in parallel plans, always multiply.
Treating a LIMIT plan as a bad estimate

Under a Limit node, child nodes show estimated cost and rows as if they ran to completion, while the actual numbers stop early. The documentation calls this a display difference, not an estimation error.
Trusting timings from EXPLAIN ANALYZE too much

Measuring the time of every node adds overhead, especially for nodes that run many times and on machines with slow clock calls. If you only need row counts, use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING OFF); the total execution time is still measured. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also does not send rows to the client, so network time and, unless you add SERIALIZE, the cost of converting results to text are not included.
Practice exercise

items.content: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date = '2026-03-15'; What kind of scan do you get, how many rows are removed by the filter, and how many buffers are used?
Create an index that fixes it, run the query again and compare the buffer counts. Then drop your index.

data.title: Answer
data.text: Without an index on order_date you get a Parallel Seq Scan that returns 1,667 rows (about 556 per process over 3 loops), removes about 182,778 rows per process by the filter and uses about 4,500 shared buffers: the whole table, which grew after the UPDATE in Step 9. After CREATE INDEX orders_order_date_idx ON orders (order_date); the plan switches to a Bitmap Index Scan plus Bitmap Heap Scan with Heap Blocks: exact=1667 and about 1,671 buffers, and the time falls from about 42 ms to about 2 ms on the test machine. The buffer saving is smaller than in Step 5 because each matching row sits on a different page. Clean up with DROP INDEX orders_order_date_idx;
Quick reference

data.caption: Every command from this part, in order

data.title: Clean up only the practice database
data.text: dropdb removes the database and all its data without asking. Check the name twice and never run it against a real database.
Summary and what's next

items.content: Plain EXPLAIN shows the estimated plan and is safe to run anywhere.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) runs the statement and shows actual time, rows, loops and pages; on PostgreSQL 18 BUFFERS is included automatically.
Read plans from the inside out and multiply per-loop numbers by loops.
A large gap between estimated and actual rows usually means stale or missing statistics; run ANALYZE.
Big Rows Removed by Filter points to a missing index; temp read/written points to work_mem; high Heap Fetches points to VACUUM.
Wrap EXPLAIN ANALYZE of INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
Use GENERIC_PLAN for queries with $1 copied from pg_stat_statements.

data.text: In Part 27 we build on these plans to choose the right index type: B-tree, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial and expression indexes.

linkedin.post:
EXPLAIN said 1 row. The query returned 50,000. That gap is where most slow PostgreSQL plans start.

Part 26 of my PostgreSQL DBA series is about reading EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) the way a DBA does:

→ Compare estimated rows with actual rows x loops on every node. A 10x gap usually means stale statistics. Run ANALYZE.
→ Buffers shared read vs shared hit tells you if pages came from disk or from cache. Compare buffers, not just milliseconds.
→ A huge "Rows Removed by Filter" on a Seq Scan is the classic missing-index sign.
→ "Sort Method: external merge" and temp read/written mean work_mem was too small for that sort.
→ High Heap Fetches on an Index Only Scan means the table needs VACUUM.

Two PostgreSQL 18 changes: BUFFERS is now included with ANALYZE automatically, and row counts show decimals, so rows=33.33 loops=3 no longer hides small numbers.

And always wrap EXPLAIN ANALYZE of an UPDATE or DELETE in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK. It really runs.

Follow the series for Part 27 on index strategy.
